summary: Describes how to carry IP datagrams, and the higher-level protocols above them, over Network Systems Corporation's HYPERchannel equipment. It targets network planners and implementors who already know TCP/IP, and includes an appendix reviewing HYPERchannel technology. It was an Internet standard and was later updated by RFC 5494.

eli5.summary: A special fast cable system for big computers had its own rules. This memo explains how to put regular Internet packets on it.

subtitle: How to carry IP datagrams, and an ARP variant, over Network Systems Corporation's HYPERchannel high-speed network.

tldr.problem: Several vendors had built incompatible ways to run IP over HYPERchannel, and the network's 16-bit addressing was running out of room for larger networks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC fixes one encapsulation for IP in the 16-bit message and a new one for the 32-bit extended message, assigns message type codes, and defines an Address Resolution Protocol with MTU exchange.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard, and the unit metadata lists RFC 5494 as having updated it.

today: RFC 1044 is an Internet Standard, and the metadata lists RFC 5494 as updating it. It is not marked as obsoleted.

sections.title: Goals of the Specification
sections.content:
RFC 1044 is written for network planners and implementors who already know TCP/IP. It describes how to embed IP datagrams, and the higher-level protocols above them, on Network Systems Corporation's (NSC) HYPERchannel equipment.

The RFC names four objectives. First, to bless a de facto standard for IP on HYPERchannel already implemented by Tektronix, Cray, NASA Ames and others, and to resolve interoperability problems in it. Second, to introduce a move from a 16-bit TO address to a 32-bit address and say how IP works in that mode. Third, to define an Address Resolution Protocol for HYPERchannel, since NSC products of the time did not support broadcast and many wanted ARP servers at a known network address. Fourth, to standardize the unofficial message type field in byte 8 of the network message, with NSC starting a network protocol registry.
sections.eli5: Many people had already found their own ways to put Internet packets on this special network, and the ways did not always match. This memo picks one way so everybody can talk to each other.

sections.title: The HYPERchannel Network Message
sections.content:
Unlike most datagram systems, a HYPERchannel network message has two parts. The Message Proper is a header of 10 to 64 bytes. The optional Associated Data follows it and is effectively unlimited in length on HYPERchannel A trunks, while HYPERchannel B and a local A400 adapter limit it to 4K bytes. If everything fits in the Message Proper, no Associated Data need be sent.

The first 10 bytes of the Message Proper are read by the network adapters to deliver the message: Trunks to Try, Message Flags, an access code, the TO address, the FROM address and the message type. The remaining bytes are free for higher-level protocols. The RFC suggests setting the trunk mask to 0xFF for maximum interoperability.

The flags carry three bits in the basic format: Associated Data present (A/D), Burst Mode (BST) and Exception (EXC). The access code is not in use and support is being discontinued. The FROM address is passed to the receiver so a reply can be sent by reversing the TO and FROM fields.

The logical part of the TO address chooses the protocol server that receives a message, so the message type cannot redirect it. RFC 1044 compares this to the OSI idea of embedding the server in the address, rather than the IP idea of addressing a host and then a protocol.
sections.eli5: Each message is like a letter with a short address card on top and an optional pile of pages behind it. If the whole message fits on the card, no pile is needed.

sections.title: 32-Bit Addressing and Broadcast
sections.content:
The original 16-bit scheme could address 256 adapters, which was considered enough when 40 or so adapters was a large network. The extended message header carries 32 bits of address, 24 of which designate a physical network adapter. A Global Network Addressing (GNA) flag says 32-bit addressing is present.

Each local collection of adapters is a network of up to 256 adapters, and a large NSC network can have up to 64K networks. The 16-bit network field is split into a domain number and a network number. Bridges check bytes 2 to 5 against masks and their own domain, network and address to decide whether to accept a message for forwarding.

Other new header fields include a CRC flag for end-to-end integrity, an SRC flag meaning the FROM address was verified, and an age count that works like the IP time to live: each bridge decrements it and discards the message when it reaches zero. A high-order 'outnet' bit in the adapter address keeps older A-series adapters from accepting messages that are merely passing through.

Broadcast exists only in the extended format. The value 0xFF in the domain, network or adapter field is reserved for it, and broadcast channel numbers 00 to 0xFF are assigned by NSC. The RFC says no current NSC implementation supports broadcast, but new technologies will.
sections.eli5: The old address could name only a small number of machines, like a street with a few houses. The new address adds a town and a region so many more machines can be found.

sections.title: Encapsulating IP Datagrams
sections.content:
In the basic 16-bit encapsulation, the sender puts the value 5 in byte 8 to mark the message as carrying IP, and no other well-behaved protocol should use it. Byte 9 and byte 11 both hold an offset to the IP header, and on reception byte 11 takes precedence. Byte 10 holds the IP type designator 0x34, which is generated on transmission but not checked on input. The offset in byte 11 is relative to byte 12, and its maximum is 52.

The IP datagram is treated as one contiguous block that flows from byte 63 of the Message Proper into the first byte of the Associated Data. The Message Proper sent is always 64 bytes. A driver should take the datagram length from the IP header, not from the length of the associated data, because some machines cannot send an exact byte count.

The 32-bit encapsulation uses the value 6 in byte 8, an extended-addressing flag, and an offset in byte 9 that receivers must trust. Valid offsets are 16 through 44 bytes, so routing decisions can be made from the Message Proper alone. Drivers tell the formats apart by byte 8: 6 means 32-bit, 5 means 16-bit, and 0 is treated as 16-bit for older drivers.

Transmitting drivers should set the end-to-end CRC bit only when the attached adapter generates CRCs. Drivers should also be prepared to accept 0xFF00 in bytes 8 and 9, which loops a message back at the destination adapter for debugging.
sections.eli5: The Internet packet is slid into the envelope, and a tag with the number 5 or 6 tells the mail room it holds Internet mail. If the packet is too big for the envelope, the rest goes in the pile behind it.

sections.title: Compatibility with Existing Drivers
sections.content:
The RFC says the basic format is a compromise and not every existing implementation interoperates with it. It identifies two families of drivers.

The Cray-NASA Ames protocol has the widest production use and is identical to the standard except that these drivers set bytes 8 and 9 to zero. The Tektronix-Berkeley protocol was the first IP on HYPERchannel, made its way to Berkeley and BSD UNIX, and is not interoperable. Its bytes 8 through 11 are always zero and the IP header always starts at byte 12. If the datagram is 54 bytes or less it is sent in the Message Proper alone; otherwise the TCP or UDP header and data go in the Associated Data.

The RFC chose the Cray-Ames approach for three reasons: several vendor-supported implementations use it, its two-part structure suits coprocessors that read the whole message first, and the Tektronix-Berkeley approach has problems when the IP header length exceeds 54 bytes, which some secure DoD sites expected from IP options.
sections.eli5: Two groups had packed their boxes in different ways. The memo picked the way most people already used, because it also works for bigger boxes.

sections.title: Address Resolution and ARP
sections.content:
An IP driver must turn an IP address into a HYPERchannel address and header. The RFC describes four approaches: truncating the IP address, local resolution from configuration files, centralized resolution through an ARP server, and distributed resolution with a real ARP on future broadcast-capable media.

Truncation places the low-order 16 bits of the IP address in the TO address. It works only when HYPERchannel is a whole Class B network, and the RFC discourages it because it fails for Class A and Class C addresses, subnetworks and 32-bit addresses. Local resolution uses a table, often hashed, whose entries hold the first 6 bytes of the HYPERchannel header. The RFC shows a configuration file with line types host, ahost, loop, address and arpserver.

Because changing a host means updating every machine's table, the RFC proposes ARP servers. A server answers only requests sent to its well-known address, ignores addresses it cannot resolve so another server can be tried, and returns the HYPERchannel address and MTU to the FROM address. Once broadcast exists, drivers can send ARP to the broadcast TO address 0xFFFFFF07 and answer only for addresses they are authoritative for, as in RFC 826. Static entries win over contradicting ARP information, because the RFC notes it is easy to lie with ARP.
sections.eli5: To mail a friend you need their street address, not just their name. A directory keeper who knows everyone's address can be asked, so each person does not have to keep a list.

sections.title: ARP Message and MTU Exchange
sections.content:
The ARP message uses the 32-bit header with message type 0x0700, reserved for ARP. Inside, the hardware address type is 8, the protocol type is 0x0600, the HYPERchannel address length is 6 and the IP address length is 4. The six address bytes are the four-byte HYPERchannel address plus two bytes giving the largest IP datagram the host can handle.

That second field carries each host's maximum transmission unit. Each host declares the largest IP datagram, not associated data block, it will receive, and senders use the minimum of the two sizes negotiated at ARP time. The MTU counts the IP header and data but not the HYPERchannel header or offset. The RFC's examples both give an MTU of 4136, built from 40 bytes of IP and TCP header plus 4096 bytes of data. The maximum is 65536, and a configuration file assumes 4148 if none is given.

ARP carries no trunk mask because new NSC hardware would know trunk reachability, so messages generated from an ARP response should use 0xFF.
sections.eli5: Before two machines swap packages, each says how big a box it can handle, and they agree to use the smaller size so nothing gets stuck.
